Thanks Marissa  good recap. A few quick answers and clarifications: 

Auth
- We prefer OIDC short-lived tokens issued by our IdP (Auth0). We can add Redwood as an OIDC client and issue tokens scoped to inference APIs.

Structured output
- We need strongly validated JSON for the assistant's actions (the frontend relies on a stable schema). However, for streaming, partial chunks are okay as long as the final assembled output validates against the schema.

Embeddings / reranker
- Typical payloads: 1k-5k docs per day, batch sizes up to 128, avg doc length ~400 tokens. Reranker will run as a follow-up call (embedding -> candidate set -> rerank).

Streaming
- Latency matters for the chat assistant; prefer streaming of partial text for UX. For structured outputs, streaming must include clear chunk boundaries or use an indexer pattern so we can reassemble deterministically.

I've attached our internal requirements doc: acme_api_requirements.xlsx. Also looping in Rajesh (cc'd) who will join the tech sync.

Schedule: Tue Oct 12 at 10:00 PT works for us.

-Alice

Great  thanks for the details and for looping Rajesh in. A few notes ahead of the tech sync and an internal task list.

Short answers to the items you called out:
- Auth: we support OIDC flows (we can accept JWTs issued by your IdP). For the short-lived-token flow we recommend using our SDK to automatically refresh tokens; Dev, please review the "OIDC client" docs in the attached SDK guide.

- Chat vs completions: for multi-turn assistant + tool calling we recommend the Chat endpoints (structured messages + tool invocation helpers). Completions are simpler and can be used for single-turn generation where you only expect text.

- Tokenization / max_tokens / stop sequences:
  * Tokenization: our SDK exposes token_count helpers for both chat and legacy completion formats. Use token_count to precompute prompt size for billing and truncation.
  * max_tokens: set max_tokens for the output; when streaming, the stream ends when final token is emitted or when max_tokens is reached. If you need hard-enforced length, set a low max_tokens and implement truncation on the client side.
  * stop: stop sequences are honored for both chat and completions; for structured JSON we recommend a schema-aware sentinel (e.g., "\n<END_JSON>\n") to avoid accidental truncation inside nested objects.

- Streaming semantics for structured output:
  * We stream delta tokens by default (tokens that incrementally build the final response). For JSON outputs we support two patterns:
    1) Chunked JSON objects: the model emits complete JSON objects delimited by a newline. Client reassembles by parsing each line as an object and appending to an array.
    2) Framed JSON stream: we emit JSON fragments with explicit metadata frames (offset, length, final=true). If you require deterministic reassembly, we recommend the framed approach.
  * Note: framed JSON requires protocol support on the client; our SDK has helpers to reassemble and validate against a schema as the stream completes.

- Embeddings / reranker: batching + async job pattern is the most cost-effective. Dev, please confirm the expected concurrency and we'll propose a batching policy (suggested: batch up to 128 vectors or 5MB payload per request).

Sample request hints (for the tech sync slide deck):
- Chat w/ tool calling (pseudo):
  POST /v1/chat:send
  body: {"model":"redwood-chat-1","messages":[{"role":"system","content":"..."},{"role":"user","content":"..."}],"stream":true,"max_tokens":512}

- Structured streaming (framed) example (high level):
  stream chunks: {"frame": {"offset":0}, "data":"{\"action\":\"open_url\",\"url\":\"https://...\"}"}
  final chunk: {"frame": {"offset":... , "final": true}}
